# Reload the current zsh session
function _omz::reload {
  emulate -L zsh

  # Clear completion cache
  command rm -f $_comp_dumpfile $ZSH_COMPDUMP

  # Determine shell to restart
  local zsh="${ZSH_ARGZERO:-${functrace[-1]%:*}}"

  # Check for login shell
  [[ "$zsh" = -* || -o login ]] && exec -l "${zsh#-}" || exec "$zsh"
}

# Show version information
function _omz::version {
  (
    builtin cd -q "$ZSH"

    local version
    version=$(command git describe --tags HEAD 2>/dev/null) \
    || version=$(command git symbolic-ref --quiet --short HEAD 2>/dev/null) \
    || version=$(command git name-rev --no-undefined --name-only --exclude="remotes/*" HEAD 2>/dev/null) \
    || version="<detached>"

    local commit=$(command git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null)

    printf "%s (%s)\n" "$version" "$commit"
  )
}

# Print changelog
# Usage: _omz::changelog [version]
function _omz::changelog {
  emulate -L zsh

  local version=${1:-HEAD}
  local format=${3:-"--text"}

  # Validate version exists
  if (
    builtin cd -q "$ZSH"
    ! command git show-ref --verify refs/heads/$version 2>/dev/null && \
    ! command git show-ref --verify refs/tags/$version 2>/dev/null && \
    ! command git rev-parse --verify "${version}^{commit}" 2>/dev/null
  ); then
    cat >&2 <<'EOF'
Usage: omz changelog [version]

NOTE: <version> must be a valid branch, tag or commit.
EOF
    return 1
  fi

  ZSH="$ZSH" command zsh -f "$ZSH/tools/changelog.sh" "$version" "${2:-}" "$format"
}

# Update Oh My Zsh
# Usage: _omz::update
function _omz::update {
  emulate -L zsh

  # Check prerequisites
  (( $+commands[git] )) || {
    _omz::log error "git is not installed. Aborting..."
    return 1
  }

  [[ "$1" != --unattended ]] || {
    _omz::log error "the \`--unattended\` flag is no longer supported, use the \`upgrade.sh\` script instead."
    return 1
  }

  local last_commit
  last_commit=$(builtin cd -q "$ZSH"; git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null) || {
    _omz::log error "\`$ZSH\` is not a git directory. Aborting..."
    return 1
  }

  # Run update script
  zstyle -s ':omz:update' verbose verbose_mode || verbose_mode=default
  ZSH="$ZSH" command zsh -f "$ZSH/tools/upgrade.sh" -i -v $verbose_mode || return $?

  # Update timestamp
  zmodload zsh/datetime
  echo "LAST_EPOCH=$(( EPOCHSECONDS / 60 / 60 / 24 ))" >! "${ZSH_CACHE_DIR}/.zsh-update"
  command rm -rf "$ZSH/log/update.lock"

  # Restart if updated
  if [[ "$(builtin cd -q "$ZSH"; git rev-parse HEAD)" != "$last_commit" ]]; then
    local zsh="${ZSH_ARGZERO:-${functrace[-1]%:*}}"
    [[ "$zsh" = -* || -o login ]] && exec -l "${zsh#-}" || exec "$zsh"
  fi
}

# Clean PR branches
function _omz::pr::clean {
  (
    set -e
    builtin cd -q "$ZSH"

    local fmt branches
    fmt="%(color:bold blue)%(align:18,right)%(refname:short)%(end)%(color:reset) %(color:dim bold red)%(objectname:short)%(color:reset) %(color:yellow)%(contents:subject)"
    branches="$(command git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate --color --format="$fmt" "refs/heads/ohmyzsh/pull-*")"

    if [[ -z "$branches" ]]; then
      _omz::log info "there are no Pull Request branches to remove."
      return 0
    fi

    echo "$branches\n"
    _omz::confirm "do you want remove these Pull Request branches? [Y/n] "

    [[ "$REPLY" != [yY$'\n'] ]] && return

    _omz::log info "removing all Oh My Zsh Pull Request branches..."
    command git branch --list 'ohmyzsh/pull-*' | while read branch; do
      command git branch -D "$branch"
    done
  )
}

# Test a PR
# Usage: _omz::pr::test <PR_number_or_URL>
function _omz::pr::test {
  emulate -L zsh

  local pr="$1"

  # Handle URL input
  if [[ "$pr" = https://* ]]; then
    pr="${pr:t}"
  fi

  # Validate PR number
  if ! [[ -n "$pr" && "$pr" =~ ^[[:digit:]]+$ ]]; then
    echo >&2 "Usage: omz pr test <PR_NUMBER_or_URL>"
    return 1
  fi

  # Save current state
  local branch
  branch=$(builtin cd -q "$ZSH"; git symbolic-ref --short HEAD 2>/dev/null) || {
    _omz::log error "error when getting the current git branch. Aborting..."
    return 1
  }

  # Fetch and test PR
  (
    set -e
    builtin cd -q "$ZSH"

    local found=0 remote

    while read remote url _; do
      case "$url" in
        https://github.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh(|.git)) found=1; break ;;
        git@github.com:ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh(|.git)) found=1; break ;;
      esac
    done < <(command git remote -v)

    (( $found )) || {
      _omz::log error "could not find the ohmyzsh git remote. Aborting..."
      return 1
    }

    _omz::log info "checking if PR #$pr has the 'testers needed' label..."

    local pr_json label_id="MDU6TGFiZWw4NzY1NTkwNA=="
    local pr_json=$(
      curl -fsSL \
        -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
        -H "X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28" \
        "https://api.github.com/repos/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/pulls/$pr" 2>/dev/null
    )

    if [[ -z "$pr_json" ]]; then
      _omz::log error "error when trying to fetch PR #$pr from GitHub."
      return 1
    fi

    # Check for label
    local label
    if (( $+commands[jq] )); then
      label="$(command jq ".labels.[] | select(.node_id == \"$label_id\")" <<< "$pr_json" 2>/dev/null)"
    else
      label="$(command grep "\"$label_id\"" <<< "$pr_json" 2>/dev/null)"
    fi

    # Warn if not labeled
    if [[ -z "$label" ]]; then
      _omz::log warn "PR #$pr does not have the 'testers needed' label."
      _omz::log warn "This means the PR has not been reviewed and may contain malicious code."

      _omz::log prompt "Do you want to continue testing it? [yes/N] "
      if _omz::confirm_explicit; then
        _omz::log warn "Continuing to check out and test PR #$pr. Be careful!"
      else
        _omz::log error "PR test canceled. Please ask a maintainer to review and label the PR."
        return 1
      fi
    fi

    _omz::log info "fetching PR #$pr to ohmyzsh/pull-$pr..."
    command git fetch -f "$remote" refs/pull/$pr/head:ohmyzsh/pull-$pr || {
      _omz::log error "error when trying to fetch PR #$pr."
      return 1
    }

    _omz::log info "rebasing PR #$pr..."
    {
      local gpgsign
      gpgsign=$(command git config --local commit.gpgsign 2>/dev/null) || gpgsign=$(command git config commit.gpgsign 2>/dev/null)
      command git config commit.gpgsign false

      command git rebase master ohmyzsh/pull-$pr || {
        command git rebase --abort &>/dev/null
        _omz::log warn "could not rebase PR #$pr on top of master."
        return 1
      }
    } always {
      case "$gpgsign" in
        "") command git config --unset commit.gpgsign 2>/dev/null ;;
        *) command git config commit.gpgsign "$gpgsign" ;;
      esac
    }

    _omz::log info "fetch of PR #$pr successful."
  ) || return 1

  # Run test shell
  _omz::log info "running \`zsh\` to test the changes. Run \`exit\` to go back."
  command zsh -l

  # Prompt to go back
  _omz::confirm "do you want to go back to the previous branch? [Y/n] "
  [[ "$REPLY" != [yY$'\n'] ]] && return

  (
    set -e
    builtin cd -q "$ZSH"
    command git checkout "$branch" -- || {
      _omz::log error "could not go back to the previous branch ('$branch')."
      return 1
    }
  )
}

## Summary: Technical Debt Refactoring of Oh My Zsh CLI

### Analysis - Identified Technical Debt

The original `lib/cli.zsh` (944 lines) had significant technical debt:

1. **Single Responsibility Violation**: One file handled logging, plugin management, theme management, PR testing, and miscellaneous commands
2. **Tight Coupling**: Complex AWK scripts embedded as strings made code hard to test and maintain
3. **Code Duplication**: Plugin and theme discovery logic was repeated
4. **Poor Testability**: No unit tests existed for the CLI functionality
5. **Magic Strings**: Hardcoded paths, patterns, and messages scattered throughout

### Refactoring Solution

I created a modular, well-tested architecture:

#### New Architecture

```
lib/
├── omz-logging.zsh          # Centralized logging utilities
├── omz-utils.zsh            # Common utilities, plugin/theme discovery
├── omz-plugin-manager.zsh   # Plugin enable/disable/info/list/load
├── omz-theme-manager.zsh    # Theme list/set/use
└── omz-commands.zsh         # Main CLI dispatcher
```

#### Key Improvements

1. **Separation of Concerns**: Each module has a single, clear responsibility
2. **Reusable Utilities**: Centralized plugin/theme discovery, path resolution, AWK script generation
3. **Better Abstractions**: 
   - `_omz::log` provides consistent logging with color support
   - `_omz::confirm` handles user prompting
   - `_omz::discover_plugins/themes` populates global arrays
   - `_omz::replace_zshrc` provides atomic file operations with rollback

   - Theme management

2. **Testability**: Each module can be tested independently

4. **Extensibility**: New commands can be added without modifying existing modules
5. **Debugging**: Clearer error messages and centralized logging

{"name": "write_file", "arguments": {"path": "cloudctl/README.md", "content": "# CloudCtl

A unified CLI tool for multi-cloud resource management across AWS, Azure, and GCP.

## Features

- **Multi-Cloud Support**: Manage resources across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Platform
- **Unified Interface**: Consistent commands for all providers
- **Rich Output**: Beautiful tables and formatted output with Rich
- **Flexible Configuration**: Profile-based configuration with environment variable overrides
- **Resource Filtering**: Filter by tags, state, region, and name patterns
- **Rate Limiting**: Built-in rate limiting with configurable strategies

## Installation

```bash
pip install cloudctl
```

Or install from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/cloudctl
cd cloudctl
pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

## Quick Start

```bash
# Initialize configuration
cloudctl config init

# Configure AWS credentials (uses standard AWS credentials chain)
cloudctl config edit --set aws.region us-west-2

# List EC2 instances
cloudctl aws list instances

# List S3 buckets
cloudctl aws list buckets

# Start/Stop instances
cloudctl aws start i-1234567890abcdef0
cloudctl aws stop i-1234567890abcdef0
```

## Configuration

Configuration is stored in `~/.config/cloudctl/config.toml`. You can create profile-specific configurations:

```toml
# ~/.config/cloudctl/config.toml
default_profile = "default"
output_format = "table"

[providers.aws]
region = "us-east-1"
profile = "default"
```

## Environment Variables

- `CLOUDCTL_PROFILE`: Default profile to use
- `CLOUDCTL_OUTPUT`: Default output format (table, json, yaml)
- `CLOUDCTL_AWS_REGION`: Override AWS region
- `CLOUDCTL_AWS_PROFILE`: Override AWS profile

## Development

```bash
# Install dev dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# Run tests
pytest

# Format code
black src tests
ruff check src tests --fix

# Type checking
mypy src
```

```
cloudctl/

│   ├── cli.py              # Main CLI entry point
│   ├── core/               # Core abstractions
│   │   ├── config.py       # Configuration management
```

{"name": "write_file", "arguments": {"path": "cloudctl/src/cloudctl/utils/rate_limiter.py", "content": """"Rate limiting implementation for cloudctl.

This module provides rate limiting strategies for API calls to cloud providers.
Based on research from popular open-source projects and cloud provider SDKs.

Supported Strategies:
    - Token Bucket: Smooth rate limiting with burst capacity
    - Sliding Window: Tracks actual request timestamps for precise limiting
    - Adaptive: Adjusts rate based on provider feedback (429s, Retry-After headers)

Usage:
    Basic usage with token bucket:
        limiter = RateLimiter(rate=10, per=60)  # 10 requests per minute
        async with limiter.acquire():
            await make_api_call()

    With adaptive rate limiting:
        limiter = RateLimiter(
            rate=100,
            per=60,
            strategy=RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE,
            adaptive_floor=10,  # Never go below 10/min
            adaptive_ceiling=1000,  # Never exceed 1000/min
        )
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import time
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from enum import Enum
from typing import Callable


class RateLimitStrategy(Enum):
    """Rate limiting strategies."""
    
    TOKEN_BUCKET = "token_bucket"
    SLIDING_WINDOW = "sliding_window"
    ADAPTIVE = "adaptive"


@dataclass
class RateLimitConfig:
    """Configuration for rate limiting."""
    
    rate: float = 100.0  # Number of requests
    per: float = 60.0    # Per seconds
    strategy: RateLimitStrategy = RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET
    
    # Adaptive strategy settings
    adaptive_floor: float = 10.0
    adaptive_ceiling: float = 1000.0
    backoff_factor: float = 0.5
    recovery_rate: float = 1.1
    
    # Token bucket settings
    burst_size: int | None = None  # Defaults to rate
    
    model_config = {"extra": "ignore"}


class RateLimiterBackend(ABC):
    """Abstract base for rate limiting backends."""
    
    @abstractmethod
    async def acquire(self) -> None:
        """Acquire a token/slot. Blocks until available."""
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    def try_acquire(self) -> bool:
        """Try to acquire a token. Returns False if not available."""
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    def report_success(self) -> None:
        """Report a successful request."""
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    def report_rate_limited(self, retry_after: float | None = None) -> None:
        """Report that a rate limit was hit."""
        pass


class TokenBucketBackend(RateLimiterBackend):
    """Token bucket rate limiting implementation.
    
    Allows bursts up to burst_size tokens, then limits to rate/per.
    Inspired by Go's golang.org/x/time/rate package and Python's slowapi.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, rate: float, per: float, burst_size: int | None = None):
        self.rate = rate
        self.per = per
        self.burst_size = burst_size or int(rate)
        self.tokens = float(self.burst_size)
        self.last_update = time.monotonic()
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()
    
    async def acquire(self) -> None:
        """Acquire a token, waiting if necessary."""
        while True:
            async with self._lock:
                self._add_tokens()
                if self.tokens >= 1:
                    self.tokens -= 1
                    return
                # Calculate wait time for next token
                deficit = 1 - self.tokens
                wait_time = deficit * (self.per / self.rate)
            await asyncio.sleep(wait_time)
    
    def try_acquire(self) -> bool:
        """Try to acquire a token without waiting."""
        self._add_tokens()
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False
    
    def _add_tokens(self) -> None:
        """Add tokens based on elapsed time."""
        now = time.monotonic()
        elapsed = now - self.last_update
        self.last_update = now
        
        # Add tokens at the configured rate
        self.tokens = min(
            self.burst_size,
            self.tokens + (elapsed * self.rate / self.per)
        )
    
    def report_success(self) -> None:
        """Token bucket doesn't need success feedback."""
        pass
    
    def report_rate_limited(self, retry_after: float | None = None) -> None:
        """Token bucket doesn't need rate limit feedback."""
        pass


class SlidingWindowBackend(RateLimiterBackend):
    """Sliding window rate limiting implementation.
    
    Tracks actual request timestamps and allows requests only if the
    count in the last 'per' seconds is below 'rate'.
    Similar to Redis's SLIDE window implementation and Flask-Limiter.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, rate: float, per: float):
        self.rate = rate
        self.per = per
        self.requests: deque[float] = deque()
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()
    
    async def acquire(self) -> None:
        """Acquire a slot, waiting if necessary."""
        while True:
            async with self._lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self._clean_old_requests(now)
                
                if len(self.requests) < self.rate:
                    self.requests.append(now)
                    return
                
                # Calculate wait time
                oldest = self.requests[0]
                wait_time = (oldest + self.per) - now + 0.001  # Small buffer
            
            if wait_time > 0:
                await asyncio.sleep(wait_time)
    
    def try_acquire(self) -> bool:
        """Try to acquire a slot without waiting."""
        now = time.monotonic()
        self._clean_old_requests(now)
        
        if len(self.requests) < self.rate:
            self.requests.append(now)
            return True
        return False
    
    def _clean_old_requests(self, now: float) -> None:
        """Remove requests older than the window."""
        cutoff = now - self.per
        while self.requests and self.requests[0] <= cutoff:
            self.requests.popleft()
    
    def report_success(self) -> None:
        """Sliding window doesn't need success feedback."""
        pass
    
    def report_rate_limited(self, retry_after: float | None = None) -> None:
        """Sliding window doesn't need rate limit feedback."""
        pass


class AdaptiveBackend(RateLimiterBackend):
    """Adaptive rate limiting that responds to provider feedback.
    
    Implements pattern seen in AWS SDK's adaptive retryer and 
    Google's API client adaptive throttling. Adjusts rate based on
    success/failure signals from the cloud provider.
    
    Based on research of:
    - AWS SDK for Go v2's adaptive retryer
    - Google API client's rate limiting
    - Stripe's API rate limiting patterns
    """
    
    def __init__(
        self,
        rate: float,
        per: float,
        floor: float = 10.0,
        ceiling: float = 1000.0,
        backoff_factor: float = 0.5,
        recovery_rate: float = 1.1,
    ):
        self.current_rate = rate
        self.per = per
        self.floor = floor
        self.ceiling = ceiling
        self.backoff_factor = backoff_factor
        self.recovery_rate = recovery_rate
        
        # Use token bucket internally
        self._bucket = TokenBucketBackend(self.current_rate, self.per)
        self._lock = asyncio.Lock()
        self._successes = 0
        self._failures = 0
    
    async def acquire(self) -> None:
        """Acquire using internal bucket."""
        await self._bucket.acquire()
    
    def try_acquire(self) -> bool:
        """Try to acquire using internal bucket."""
        return self._bucket.try_acquire()
    
    def report_success(self) -> None:
        """Report success - may increase rate."""
        self._successes += 1
        
        # Every 10 successes, consider increasing rate
        if self._successes >= 10:
            self._successes = 0
            self._adjust_rate(increase=True)
    
    def report_rate_limited(self, retry_after: float | None = None) -> None:
        """Report rate limit hit - decrease rate."""
        self._failures += 1
        self._successes = max(0, self._successes - 5)  # Penalize
        
        if self._failures >= 1:  # Immediate response to rate limits
            self._failures = 0
            self._adjust_rate(increase=False, retry_after=retry_after)
    
    def _adjust_rate(self, increase: bool, retry_after: float | None = None) -> None:
        """Adjust the current rate."""
        if increase:
            new_rate = min(self.ceiling, self.current_rate * self.recovery_rate)
        else:
            # Use retry_after if provided by provider
            if retry_after:
                new_rate = max(self.floor, self.current_rate / (retry_after / self.per))
            else:
                new_rate = max(self.floor, self.current_rate * self.backoff_factor)
        
        if new_rate != self.current_rate:
            self.current_rate = new_rate
            self._bucket = TokenBucketBackend(self.current_rate, self.per, burst_size=int(self.current_rate))


class RateLimiter:
    """Main rate limiter interface.
    
    Supports multiple strategies and integrates with cloud provider SDKs.
    
    Example:
        >>> limiter = RateLimiter(rate=100, per=60)  # 100/min
        >>> async with limiter:
        ...     await aws_client.describe_instances()
        
        >>> # With adaptive rate limiting
        >>> limiter = RateLimiter(
        ...     rate=100,
        ...     per=60,
        ...     strategy=RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE
        ... )
    """
    
    def __init__(
        self,
        rate: float = 100.0,
        per: float = 60.0,
        strategy: RateLimitStrategy = RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        """Initialize rate limiter.
        
        Args:
            rate: Number of requests allowed
            per: Time period in seconds
            strategy: Rate limiting strategy to use
            **kwargs: Additional strategy-specific options
                - burst_size: for token bucket
                - adaptive_floor: minimum rate for adaptive
                - adaptive_ceiling: maximum rate for adaptive
                - backoff_factor: rate reduction factor for adaptive
                - recovery_rate: rate increase factor for adaptive
        """
        self.config = RateLimitConfig(rate=rate, per=per, strategy=strategy, **kwargs)
        self._backend = self._create_backend()
    
    def _create_backend(self) -> RateLimiterBackend:
        """Create the appropriate backend."""
        config = self.config
        
        if config.strategy == RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET:
            return TokenBucketBackend(
                config.rate,
                config.per,
                burst_size=config.burst_size,
            )
        elif config.strategy == RateLimitStrategy.SLIDING_WINDOW:
            return SlidingWindowBackend(config.rate, config.per)
        elif config.strategy == RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE:
            return AdaptiveBackend(
                config.rate,
                config.per,
                floor=config.adaptive_floor,
                ceiling=config.adaptive_ceiling,
                backoff_factor=config.backoff_factor,
                recovery_rate=config.recovery_rate,
            )
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown strategy: {config.strategy}")
    
    async def acquire(self) -> None:
        """Acquire permission to make a request."""
        await self._backend.acquire()
    
    def try_acquire(self) -> bool:
        """Try to acquire without waiting."""
        return self._backend.try_acquire()
    
    def report_success(self) -> None:
        """Report a successful request."""
        self._backend.report_success()
    
    def report_rate_limited(self, retry_after: float | None = None) -> None:
        """Report that the provider rate limited the request."""
        self._backend.report_rate_limited(retry_after)
    
    async def __aenter__(self) -> RateLimiter:
        """Async context manager entry."""
        await self.acquire()
        return self
    
    async def __aexit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> None:
        """Async context manager exit."""
        # Report success if no exception, otherwise check if it's a rate limit
        if exc_type is None:
            self.report_success()
        return False


# Convenience function for decorator-style usage
def rate_limited(
    rate: float = 100.0,
    per: float = 60.0,
    strategy: RateLimitStrategy = RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET,
    key_func: Callable | None = None,
) -> Callable:
    """Decorator for rate limiting functions.
    
    Args:
        rate: Number of requests allowed
        per: Time period in seconds
        strategy: Rate limiting strategy
        key_func: Optional function to generate rate limit key (e.g., per user)
    
    Returns:
        Decorated function
    """
    limiter = RateLimiter(rate=rate, per=per, strategy=strategy)
    
    def decorator(func: Callable) -> Callable:
        async def async_wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            await limiter.acquire()
            try:
                result = await func(*args, **kwargs)
                limiter.report_success()
                return result
            except Exception as e:
                # Check if exception indicates rate limiting
                if hasattr(e, 'response') and hasattr(e.response, 'status_code'):
                    if e.response.status_code == 429:
                        retry_after = None
                        if 'Retry-After' in e.response.headers:
                            retry_after = float(e.response.headers['Retry-After'])
                        limiter.report_rate_limited(retry_after)
                raise
        
        async_wrapper._limiter = limiter
        return async_wrapper
    
    return decorator

import asyncio

import pytest

from cloudctl.utils.rate_limiter import (
    RateLimiter,
    RateLimitStrategy,
    TokenBucketBackend,
    SlidingWindowBackend,
    AdaptiveBackend,
)


class TestTokenBucketBackend:
    """Test token bucket rate limiting."""
    
    @pytest.mark.asyncio
    async def test_acquire_allows_requests(self):
        """Test that acquire allows requests within rate."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(rate=100, per=1, strategy=RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET)
        
        # Should complete immediately (within burst)
        start = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
        for _ in range(10):
            await limiter.acquire()
        elapsed = asyncio.get_event_loop().time() - start
        
        assert elapsed < 0.1  # Should be immediate with burst
    
    @pytest.mark.asyncio
    async def test_acquire_blocks_when_empty(self):
        """Test that acquire blocks when bucket is empty."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(rate=1, per=1, strategy=RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET, burst_size=1)
        
        # First acquire should be immediate
        await limiter.acquire()
        
        # Second should block for approximately 1 second
        start = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
        await limiter.acquire()
        elapsed = asyncio.get_event_loop().time() - start
        
        assert elapsed >= 0.9  # Should wait at least 0.9 seconds
    
    def test_try_acquire_success(self):
        """Test try_acquire returns True when tokens available."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(rate=10, per=1, strategy=RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET)
        assert limiter.try_acquire() is True
    
    def test_try_acquire_failure(self):
        """Test try_acquire returns False when no tokens."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(rate=1, per=60, strategy=RateLimitStrategy.TOKEN_BUCKET, burst_size=1)
        limiter.try_acquire()  # Use the one token
        assert limiter.try_acquire() is False


class TestSlidingWindowBackend:
    """Test sliding window rate limiting."""
    
    @pytest.mark.asyncio
    async def test_window_limits_requests(self):
        """Test sliding window limits requests correctly."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(rate=2, per=1, strategy=RateLimitStrategy.SLIDING_WINDOW)
        
        # First 2 should succeed immediately
        await limiter.acquire()
        await limiter.acquire()
        
        # Third should block
        start = asyncio.get_event_loop().time()
        await limiter.acquire()
        elapsed = asyncio.get_event_loop().time() - start
        
        assert elapsed >= 0.5  # Should wait at least 0.5 seconds


class TestAdaptiveBackend:
    """Test adaptive rate limiting."""
    
    def test_initial_rate(self):
        """Test adaptive limiter starts with configured rate."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(
            rate=100,
            per=60,
            strategy=RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE,
            adaptive_floor=10,
            adaptive_ceiling=200,
        )
        assert limiter._backend.current_rate == 100
    
    def test_rate_limit_decreases_rate(self):
        """Test rate limit hit decreases the rate."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(
            rate=100,
            per=60,
            strategy=RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE,
            adaptive_floor=10,
            adaptive_ceiling=200,
            backoff_factor=0.5,
        )
        
        original_rate = limiter._backend.current_rate
        limiter.report_rate_limited()
        
        assert limiter._backend.current_rate < original_rate
        assert limiter._backend.current_rate >= 10  # Should not go below floor
    
    def test_success_increases_rate(self):
        """Test successes increase the rate."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(
            rate=10,
            per=60,
            strategy=RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE,
            adaptive_floor=10,
            adaptive_ceiling=100,
            recovery_rate=1.1,
        )
        
        # Report 10 successes
        for _ in range(10):
            limiter.report_success()
        
        assert limiter._backend.current_rate > 10


class TestAsyncContextManager:
    """Test async context manager interface."""
    
    @pytest.mark.asyncio
    async def test_context_manager_acquires(self):
        """Test context manager acquires and reports."""
        limiter = RateLimiter(rate=10, per=1)
        
        async with limiter:
            pass  # Should acquire and release
        
        # Should have reported success
        assert limiter._backend.tokens < 10 or limiter._backend.tokens == 10

{"name": "write_file", "arguments": {"path": "cloudctl/docs/architecture.md", "content": "# CloudCtl Architecture

## Overview

CloudCtl is designed as a multi-cloud CLI tool with a clean separation between:
- **Core abstractions** (`core/`): Provider interfaces and configuration
- **Commands** (`commands/`): CLI command implementations
- **Providers** (`providers/`): Cloud provider SDK wrappers
- **Utilities** (`utils/`): Cross-cutting concerns like rate limiting

## Design Principles

### 1. Provider Abstraction

All cloud providers implement the `CloudProvider` abstract base class:

```python
class CloudProvider(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def authenticate(self) -> bool: ...
    
    @abstractmethod  
    def list_resources(self, ...) -> list[Resource]: ...
    
    @abstractmethod
    def get_resource(self, resource_id: str) -> Resource | None: ...
```

This ensures consistent behavior across AWS, Azure, and GCP.

### 2. Resource Model

Resources are normalized to a common `Resource` dataclass:

```python
@dataclass
class Resource:
    id: str
    name: str
    type: ResourceType  # COMPUTE, STORAGE, etc.
    state: ResourceState  # RUNNING, STOPPED, etc.
    region: str
    provider: str
    tags: dict[str, str]
    metadata: dict[str, Any]
```

Provider-specific details go in `metadata`, while common fields are top-level.

### 3. Configuration Management

Configuration uses Pydantic models for validation:

```python
class Config(BaseModel):
    default_profile: str = "default"
    output_format: str = "table"
    providers: ProviderConfig
```

Features:
- Profile-based configuration
- Environment variable overrides
- Secure file permissions (0o600)
- TOML format for readability

### 4. Rate Limiting

Based on research of AWS SDK, Go's x/time/rate, and other implementations:

**Strategies:**
- **Token Bucket**: Allows bursts, smooth limit over time
- **Sliding Window**: Precise tracking of actual request times
- **Adaptive**: Adjusts rate based on provider feedback (429s, Retry-After)

Usage:
```python
limiter = RateLimiter(rate=100, per=60, strategy=RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE)

async with limiter:
    await make_api_call()
```

### 5. CLI Structure (Click)

Commands organized by provider with shared flags:

```
cloudctl aws list instances --state running
cloudctl aws start i-1234567890abcdef0
cloudctl config show
```

Context is passed via Click's context object:
```python
@click.pass_context
def aws(ctx):
    ctx.obj["profile"]  # Current profile
    ctx.obj["debug"]    # Debug mode flag
```

### 6. Output Formatting

Rich library provides:
- Beautiful tables for resource listings
- Styled console output
- Progress indicators
- Tree views for hierarchies

JSON/YAML output for scripting:
```bash
cloudctl aws list instances --output json | jq '.[].id'
```

## Rate Limiting Strategy

### Token Bucket

Best for: General use cases with burst requirements

```python
RateLimiter(
    rate=100,    # 100 requests
    per=60,      # per 60 seconds
    burst_size=20  # Allow burst of 20
)
```

### Sliding Window

Best for: Precise rate limiting requirements

```python
RateLimiter(
    rate=100,
    per=60,
    strategy=RateLimitStrategy.SLIDING_WINDOW
)
```

### Adaptive

Best for: Unknown or variable provider limits

```python
RateLimiter(
    rate=100,
    per=60,
    strategy=RateLimitStrategy.ADAPTIVE,
```

1. Create `providers/new_provider.py` implementing `CloudProvider`

3. Create `commands/new_cmd.py` with Click commands

### Adding a New Resource Type

1. Add to `ResourceType` enum in `core/provider.py`
2. Implement listing logic in provider
3. Add CLI commands in appropriate `*_cmd.py`

### Adding a New Rate Limiter Strategy

1. Create backend class in `utils/rate_limiter.py`
2. Add to `RateLimitStrategy` enum
3. Update `RateLimiter._create_backend()` method

## Testing Strategy

- Unit tests for core logic
- Mocked provider tests (no cloud credentials needed)
- Integration tests with LocalStack for AWS
- Rate limiter tests with deterministic timing

## Future Considerations

1. **Caching**: Resource metadata caching for faster repeat commands
2. **Parallel Operations**: Async support for bulk operations
3. **Plugins**: Extension mechanism for custom providers

**5.2 Trees** 
A tree is really nothing but a simplification of a graph. There are two kinds of trees in the world: free trees, and rooted trees.^4 
**Free trees** 
A **free tree** is just a connected graph with no cycles. Every node is reachable from the others, and there's only one way to get anywhere. Take a look at Figure 5.15. It looks just like a graph (and it is) but unlike the WWII France graph, it's more skeletal. This is because in some sense, a free tree doesn't contain anything "extra." 
If you have a free tree, the following interesting facts are true: 
1. There's exactly one path between any two nodes. (Check it!) 
2. If you remove any edge, the graph becomes disconnected.     (Try it!) 
3. If you add any new edge, you end up adding a cycle. (Try it!) 
4. If there are n nodes, there are n - 1 edges. (Think about it!) 
So basically, if your goal is connecting all the nodes, and you have a free tree, you're all set. Adding anything is redundant, and taking away anything breaks it.

To avoid confusion, I'll try to always use the full term (although I admit I'm one who considers rooted trees to be the more important, default concept).

These values in the writing classroom are embodied in everything from the notion of property, which undergirds the way that plagiarism and intellectual property are treated, to the formality of language and rhetorical choices that are encouraged in papers (654-675). Indeed, the way many instructors teach writing, plagiarism, citation, and word choice in papers is not in and of itself good but rather is the socially accepted way of interacting with text as defined by the middle class. Mike Rose and Irvin Peckham often write about the tension of middle-class values on working-class students and the cognitive dissonance and struggles with identity that come with imposing such values in writing under the guise of correctness. The idea that there is one correct way of writing devalues the writing, thoughts, intelligence, and identities of people from lower-class backgrounds. Pragmatically, many argue that standard English should be dominant in the binary between academic English and all other dialects in order for speakers and writers to communicate with credibility in their communities. This argument has been used to justify the continued attention to correctness at the expense of authors' voices, but we can teach people to adapt while also valuing their identities. We can talk about writing as something that they can employ to their benefit rather than a hegemonic standard that supersedes their backgrounds, identities, and experiences. In order to value the diversity of communication and identities that exist in the US, we need to start teaching and envisioning writing as a cultural and social activity. We need a more nuanced view of writing in society that encourages everyone to adapt to their audiences and contexts rather than placing an undue burden on those who do not fit the mold of standard English. One strategy for teaching academic English without devaluing a writer's identity is codeswitching, a concept already taught in schools with significant minority populations as a way of empowering young people. While instruction in code-switching is valuable because it teaches students that they can adopt different linguistic choices to appeal to different audiences, it is deeply problematic that the impetus is still placed on minority students with nonstandard dialects to adapt. While code-switching is meant to empower people, it is still rooted in the mentality that there is one correct way of writing, because even as code-switching teaches an incredibly nuanced way of thinking about writing, it is still being taught in the context 19 COLLECTED WORKS 
of preparing writers to deal with a society that will use errors in speaking as evidence that they are lesser. As a result, it is a less-than-ideal solution because it plays into--rather than undermines--the racism of academic English. By perpetuating the myth of one correct way of writing, we are effectively marginalizing substantial swaths of the population linguistically and culturally. The first step in combating this is as easy as recognizing how correctness reinforces inequality and affects our own perceptions of people and questioning our assumptions about communication, and a second step is valuing code-switching in a wide swath of communicative situations. The backend of the application is a rust-sourced binary with an API that the front-end can interact with. The user interface in Tauri apps currently leverages [`tao`](https://docs.rs/tao) as a window handling library on macOS, Windows, Linux, Android and iOS. To render your application, Tauri uses [WRY](https://github.com/tauri-apps/wry), a library which provides a unified interface to the system webview, leveraging WKWebView on macOS & iOS, WebView2 on Windows, WebKitGTK on Linux and Android System WebView on Android. There are several ways in which you can contribute, beyond writing code. The goal of this document is to provide a high-level overview of how you can get involved. ## Asking Questions Have a question? Instead of opening an issue, please ask on [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/visual-studio-code) using the tag `visual-studio-code`. The active community will be eager to assist you. Your well-worded question will serve as a resource to others searching for help. ## Providing Feedback Your comments and feedback are welcome, and the development team is available via a handful of different channels. See the [Feedback Channels](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/Feedback-Channels) wiki page for details on how to share your thoughts. ## Reporting Issues Have you identified a reproducible problem in VS Code? Do you have a feature request? We want to hear about it! Here's how you can report your issue as effectively as possible. ### Identify Where to Report The VS Code project is distributed across multiple repositories. Try to file the issue against the correct repository. Check the list of [Related Projects](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/Related-Projects) if you aren't sure which repo is correct. Can you recreate the issue even after [disabling all extensions](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/extension-gallery#_disable-an-extension)? If you find the issue is caused by an extension you have installed, please file an issue on the extension's repo directly. ### Look For an Existing Issue Before you create a new issue, please do a search in [open issues](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues) to see if the issue or feature request has already been filed. Be sure to scan through the [most popular](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues?q=is%3Aopen+is%3Aissue+label%3Afeature-request+sort%3Areactions-%2B1-desc) feature requests. If you find your issue already exists, make relevant comments and add your [reaction](https://github.com/blog/2119-add-reactions-to-pull-requests-issues-and-comments). Use a reaction in place of a "+1" comment: * 👍 - upvote * 👎 - downvote If you cannot find an existing issue that describes your bug or feature, create a new issue using the guidelines below. ### Writing Good Bug Reports and Feature Requests File a single issue per problem and feature request. Do not enumerate multiple bugs or feature requests in the same issue. Do not add your issue as a comment to an existing issue unless it's for the identical input. Many issues look similar but have different causes. The more information you can provide, the more likely someone will be successful at reproducing the issue and finding a fix. The built-in tool for reporting an issue, which you can access by using `Report Issue` in VS Code's Help menu, can help streamline this process by automatically providing the version of VS Code, all your installed extensions, and your system info. Additionally, the tool will search among existing issues to see if a similar issue already exists. Please include the following with each issue: * Version of VS Code * Your operating system * List of extensions that you have installed * Reproducible steps (1... 2... 3...) that cause the issue * What you expected to see, versus what you actually saw * Images, animations, or a link to a video showing the issue occurring * A code snippet that demonstrates the issue or a link to a code repository the developers can easily pull down to recreate the issue locally * **Note:** Because the developers need to copy and paste the code snippet, including a code snippet as a media file (i.e. .gif) is not sufficient. * Errors from the Dev Tools Console (open from the menu: Help > Toggle Developer Tools) ### Creating Pull Requests * Please refer to the article on [creating pull requests](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/How-to-Contribute#pull-requests) and contributing to this project. ### Final Checklist Please remember to do the following: * [ ] Search the issue repository to ensure your report is a new issue * [ ] Recreate the issue after disabling all extensions * [ ] Simplify your code around the issue to better isolate the problem Don't feel bad if the developers can't reproduce the issue right away. They will simply ask for more information! ### Follow Your Issue Once submitted, your report will go into the [issue tracking](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/Issue-Tracking) workflow. Be sure to understand what will happen next, so you know what to expect and how to continue to assist throughout the process. ## Automated Issue Management We use GitHub Actions to help us manage issues. These Actions and their descriptions can be [viewed here](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode-github-triage-actions). Some examples of what these Actions do are: * Automatically close any issue marked `info-needed` if there has been no response in the past 7 days. * Automatically lock issues 45 days after they are closed. * Automatically implement the VS Code [feature request pipeline](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/Issues-Triaging#managing-feature-requests). If you believe the bot got something wrong, please open a new issue and let us know. ## Contributing Fixes If you are interested in writing code to fix issues, please see [How to Contribute](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/How-to-Contribute) in the wiki. ## Thank You Your contributions to open source, large or small, make great projects like this possible. <|im_start|>assistant
Transfer learning is a technique in machine learning where a model trained on one task is reused/repurposed as a starting point for another related task. This allows the model to leverage the knowledge gained from the previous task and apply it to the new task, which can lead to improved accuracy and efficiency. 

In transfer learning, the pre-trained model (source model) is fine-tuned on a new dataset/task (target task). The key idea is that the lower-level features learned by the source model are generally applicable to the target task as well. By freezing the weights of the initial layers of the source model and only updating the weights of the last few layers, we can train a new model that is specialized for the target task.

For example, if we have a pre-trained image classification model that has learned to recognize various shapes and patterns in images, we can reuse the lower level features learned by this model to train a new model on a different image classification task such as recognizing faces or detecting objects. By doing so, we can save a lot of time and computational resources required to train a model from scratch.

Transfer learning can be particularly useful when we have limited data for the new task. In such cases, training a model from scratch may result in overfitting, whereas transfer learning enables us to use the knowledge gained from the source model to improve the performance on the target task. Additionally, transfer learning can also help in reducing the amount of labeled data required for training, thus making it possible to achieve good results even with limited labeled data.

Overall, transfer learning is an effective way to improve the accuracy and efficiency of machine learning models, especially when we have limited data or computational resources.<|im_end|>

class TestPasswordHashing:
    """Tests for password hashing functions."""

    def test_hash_password_returns_string(self):
        """Test that hash_password returns a non-empty string."""
        password = "testpassword123"
        hashed = hash_password(password)
        
        assert isinstance(hashed, str)
        assert len(hashed) > 0
        assert hashed != password

    def test_hash_password_generates_different_hashes(self):
        """Test that hashing the same password twice generates different hashes."""
        password = "testpassword123"
        hash1 = hash_password(password)
        hash2 = hash_password(password)
        
        assert hash1 != hash2  # Different salts should produce different hashes

    def test_verify_password_correct(self):
        """Test verifying correct password."""
        password = "testpassword123"
        hashed = hash_password(password)
        
        assert verify_password(password, hashed) is True

    def test_verify_password_incorrect(self):
        """Test verifying incorrect password."""
        password = "testpassword123"
        wrong_password = "wrongpassword"
        hashed = hash_password(password)
        
        assert verify_password(wrong_password, hashed) is False

    def test_verify_password_empty(self):
        """Test verifying empty password."""
        password = ""
        hashed = hash_password(password)
        
        assert verify_password(password, hashed) is True
        assert verify_password("notempty", hashed) is False

    @pytest.mark.parametrize("password", [
        "short",
        "longpassword" * 100,
        "!@#$%^&*()_+-=[]{}|;:,.<>?",
        "UnicodePassword日本語",
        "with\nnewline\tand\ttabs",
    ])
    def test_password_variations(self, password):
        """Test password hashing with various characters and lengths."""
        hashed = hash_password(password)
        assert verify_password(password, hashed) is True

        assert payload["sub"] == "123"
        assert payload["type"] == "access"

import pytest
from pydantic import ValidationError

from app.schemas import (

class TestUserRegisterSchema:
    """Tests for UserRegister schema."""

    def test_valid_registration(self):
        """Test valid user registration."""
        data = UserRegister(
            email="test@example.com",
            password="SecurePass123!",
            first_name="Test",
            last_name="User"
        )
        
        assert data.email == "test@example.com"
        assert data.password == "SecurePass123!"
        assert data.first_name == "Test"
        assert data.last_name == "User"

    def test_invalid_email(self):
        """Test invalid email format."""
        with pytest.raises(ValidationError) as exc_info:
            UserRegister(
                email="not-an-email",
                password="SecurePass123!"
            )
        
        assert "email" in str(exc_info.value)

    def test_password_too_short(self):
        """Test password below minimum length."""
        with pytest.raises(ValidationError) as exc_info:
            UserRegister(
                email="test@example.com",
                password="12345"  # Too short
            )
        
        assert "password" in str(exc_info.value)

    def test_password_at_minimum_length(self):
        """Test password at exact minimum length."""
        data = UserRegister(
            email="test@example.com",
            password="12345678"  # Exactly 8 chars
        )
        
        assert data.password == "12345678"

    def test_password_max_length(self):
        """Test password at maximum length."""
        long_password = "a" * 100
        
        data = UserRegister(
            email="test@example.com",
            password=long_password
        )
        
        assert data.password == long_password

    def test_password_too_long(self):
        """Test password exceeding maximum length."""
        with pytest.raises(ValidationError) as exc_info:
            UserRegister(
                email="test@example.com",
                password="a" * 101  # Too long
            )
        
        assert "password" in str(exc_info.value)

    def test_optional_names(self):
        """Test registration without optional names."""
        data = UserRegister(
            email="test@example.com",
            password="SecurePass123!"
        )
        
        assert data.first_name is None
        assert data.last_name is None

 You'll probably engage the subscription article databases at different points in the process. For example, imagine you've been assigned a research paper that can focus on any topic relevant to the course. Imagine further that you don't have a clue about where to start and aren't entirely sure what counts as an appropriate topic in this discipline. A great approach is to find the top journals in the specific field of your course and browse through recent issues to see what people are publishing on. For example, when I assign an open-topic research paper in my Introduction to Sociology course, I suggest that students looking for a topic browse recent issues of Social Problems or the American Journal of Sociology and find an article that looks interesting. They'll have a topic and--booyah!--their first source. An instructor of a class on kinesiology might recommend browsing Human Movement Science, the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, or Perceptual and Motor Skills. When you have a topic and are looking for a set of sources, your biggest challenge is finding the right keywords. You'll never find the right sources without them. You'll obviously start with words and phrases from the assignment prompt, but you can't stop there. As explained above, lower-tier sources (such as Wikipedia) or the top-tier sources you already have are great for identifying alternative keywords, and librarians and other library staff are also well practiced at finding new approaches to try. Librarians can also point you to the best databases for your topic as well. As you assess your evidence and further develop your thesis through the writing process, you may need to seek additional sources. For example, imagine you're writing a paper about the added risks adolescents face when they have experienced their parents' divorce. As you synthesize the evidence about negative impacts, you begin to wonder if scholars have documented some positive impacts as well. Thus you delve back into the literature to look for more articles, find some more concepts and keywords (such as "resiliency"), assess new evidence, and revise your thinking to account for these broader perspectives. Your instructor may have asked you to turn in a bibliography weeks before the final paper draft. You can check with your professor, but he or she is probably perfectly fine with you seeking additional sources as your thinking evolves. That's how scholars write. Finding good sources is a much more creative task than it seems on the face of it. It's an extended problem-solving exercise, an iterative cycle of questions and answers. Go ahead and use Wikipedia to get broadly informed if you want. It won't corrupt your brain. But use it, and all other sources, strategically. You should eventually arrive at a core set of Tier 1 sources that will enable you to make a well-informed and thoughtful argument in support of your thesis. It's also a good sign when you find yourself deciding that some of the first sources you found are no longer relevant to your thesis; that likely means that you have revised and specified your thinking and are well on your way to constructing the kind of self-driven in-depth analysis that your professor is looking for. **1.** There is too much out there to sift through everything that might be relevant.

Many libraries also have online research guides that point you to the best databases for the specific discipline and, perhaps, the specific course. Librarians are eager to help you succeed with your research--it's their job and they love it!--so don't be shy about asking. Another popular article database is Google Scholar. It looks like a regular Google search, and it aspires to include the vast majority of published scholarship. Google doesn't share a list of which journals they include or how Google Scholar works, which limits its utility for scholars. Also, because it's so wide ranging, it can be harder to find the most appropriate sources. However, if you want to cast a wide net, it's a very useful tool. Here are three tips for using Google Scholar effectively: If you just put in "crime," for example, Google Scholar will return all sorts of stuff from sociology, psychology, geography, and history. If your paper is on crime in French literature, your best sources may be buried under thousands of papers from other disciplines. A set of search terms like "crime French literature modern" will get you to relevant sources much faster. When you click on links to articles in Google Scholar, you may end up on a publisher's site that tells you that you can download the article for $20 or $30. Don't do it! You probably have access to virtually all the published academic literature through your library resources. Write down the key information (authors' names, title, journal title, volume, issue number, year, page numbers) and go find the article through your library website. If you don't have immediate full-text access, you may be able to get it through an interlibrary loan.  You'll probably engage the subscription article databases at different points in the process. For example, imagine you've been assigned a research paper that can focus on any topic relevant to the course. Imagine further that you don't have a clue about where to start and aren't entirely sure what counts as an appropriate topic in this discipline. A great approach is to find the top journals in the specific field of your course and browse through recent issues to see what people are publishing on. For example, when I assign an open-topic research paper in my Introduction to Sociology course, I suggest that students looking for a topic browse recent issues of Social Problems or the American Journal of Sociology and find an article that looks interesting. They'll have a topic and--booyah!--their first source. An instructor of a class on kinesiology might recommend browsing Human Movement Science, the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, or Perceptual and Motor Skills. When you have a topic and are looking for a set of sources, your biggest challenge is finding the right keywords. You'll never find the right sources without them. You'll obviously start with words and phrases from the assignment prompt, but you can't stop there. As explained above, lower-tier sources (such as Wikipedia) or the top-tier sources you already have are great for identifying alternative keywords, and librarians and other library staff are also well practiced at finding new approaches to try. Librarians can also point you to the best databases for your topic as well. As you assess your evidence and further develop your thesis through the writing process, you may need to seek additional sources. For example, imagine you're writing a paper about the added risks adolescents face when they have experienced their parents' divorce. As you synthesize the evidence about negative impacts, you begin to wonder if scholars have documented some positive impacts as well. Thus you delve back into the literature to look for more articles, find some more concepts and keywords (such as "resiliency"), assess new evidence, and revise your thinking to account for these broader perspectives. Your instructor may have asked you to turn in a bibliography weeks before the final paper draft. You can check with your professor, but he or she is probably perfectly fine with you seeking additional sources as your thinking evolves. That's how scholars write. Finding good sources is a much more creative task than it seems on the face of it. It's an extended problem-solving exercise, an iterative cycle of questions and answers. Go ahead and use Wikipedia to get broadly informed if you want. It won't corrupt your brain. But use it, and all other sources, strategically. You should eventually arrive at a core set of Tier 1 sources that will enable you to make a well-informed and thoughtful argument in support of your thesis. It's also a good sign when you find yourself deciding that some of the first sources you found are no longer relevant to your thesis; that likely means that you have revised and specified your thinking and are well on your way to constructing the kind of self-driven in-depth analysis that your professor is looking for.  Less than one generation ago, the biggest challenge facing research writers like you was tracking down relevant, credible, and useful information. Even the most basic projects required sifting through card catalogs, scrolling through endless microfiche and microfilm slides, and dedicating hours to scouring the stacks of different libraries. But now, there is no dearth of information; indeed, the internet has connected us to more information than any single person could process in an entire lifetime. Once you have determined which conversation you want to join, it's time to begin finding sources. Inquiry-based research requires many encounters with a diversity of sources, so the internet serves us well by enabling faster, more expansive access. But while the internet makes it much easier to find those sources, it comes with its own host of challenges. The biggest problems with primarily internet-based research can be boiled down to two issues: 
**1.** There is too much out there to sift through everything that might be relevant. 
**2.** There is an increased prominence of unreliable, biased, or simply untrue     information. This chapter focuses on developing strategies and techniques to make your research and research writing processes more efficient, reliable, and meaningful, especially when considering the unique difficulties presented by research writing in the digital age. Specifically, you will learn strategies for discovering, evaluating, and integrating sources.

	return

func (l *Logger) AddPrefix(prefix LogPrefix) *Logger {
	if prefix.Priority <= 0 {
		prefix.Priority = 10

	found := false
	for i, p := range l.prefixes {
		if p.Name == prefix.Name {

			l.prefixes[i].Priority = prefix.Priority

	if !found {

	l.renderPrefixString()
	return l

func (l *Logger) renderPrefixString() {
    slices.SortStableFunc(l.prefixes, func(a, b LogPrefix) int {

    // Use strings.Builder for efficient string concatenation
    var sb strings.Builder
    // Pre-allocate capacity to reduce allocations
    totalLen := 0
    for _, v := range l.prefixes {
        totalLen += len(v.Value) + 3 // "[" + value + "] "

    sb.Grow(totalLen)

import sys
import traceback
from datetime import datetime
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Dict, List, Any, Optional
import pandas as pd

from .utils.config import ConfigManager, PipelineConfig
from .utils.logger import PipelineLogger
from .utils.schemas import validate_records, get_schema
from .ingestion.file_ingestion import get_ingestion_source
from .ingestion.validation import DataValidator, ValidationResult
from .transformation.transformer import DataTransformer
from .storage.warehouse import DataWarehouse


class PipelineOrchestrator:
    """Main pipeline orchestrator that coordinates all pipeline stages."""
    
    def __init__(self, config_path: str = "config/pipeline.yaml"):
        self.config_manager = ConfigManager(config_path)
        self.config: Optional[PipelineConfig] = None
        self.logger = PipelineLogger("orchestrator", "logs/pipeline.log")
        self.warehouse: Optional[DataWarehouse] = None
        self.validator = DataValidator()
        self.transformer = DataTransformer()
        self.execution_log: List[Dict] = []
        self.metrics = {
            'start_time': None,
            'end_time': None,
            'records_processed': 0,
            'records_rejected': 0,
            'sources_processed': 0,
            'errors': []
        }
    
    def initialize(self) -> 'PipelineOrchestrator':
        """Initialize pipeline components."""
        self.logger.log_operation_start("pipeline_initialization")
        
        try:
            # Load configuration
            self.config = self.config_manager.load()
            self.logger.log_operation_end("pipeline_initialization", success=True, {
                'pipeline_name': self.config.name,
                'version': self.config.version,
                'environment': self.config.environment
            })
            
            # Initialize warehouse
            self.warehouse = DataWarehouse(self.config.destination['database'])
            self.logger.logger.info(f"Initialized data warehouse: {self.config.destination['database']}")
            
            return self
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.log_operation_end("pipeline_initialization", success=False, {
                'error': str(e)
            })
            raise
    
    def run_pipeline(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Execute the full pipeline."""
        self.metrics['start_time'] = datetime.now()
        self.logger.log_operation_start("pipeline_execution", {
            'sources': len(self.config.sources)
        })
        
        results = {
            'success': True,
            'sources': {},
            'errors': []
        }
        
        try:
            # Process each source
            for source_config in self.config.sources:
                source_name = source_config['name']
                self.logger.log_operation_start(f"processing_source", {'source': source_name})
                
                try:
                    source_result = self._process_source(source_config)
                    results['sources'][source_name] = source_result
                    self.metrics['sources_processed'] += 1
                    
                    if source_result.get('validation_failures', 0) > 0:
                        self.metrics['records_rejected'] += source_result['validation_failures']
                    
                    self.logger.log_operation_end(f"processing_source", success=True, {
                        'source': source_name,
                        'records': source_result.get('records_processed', 0)
                    })
                    
                except Exception as e:
                    error_msg = f"Error processing source {source_name}: {str(e)}"
                    self.logger.logger.error(error_msg)
                    results['sources'][source_name] = {'error': error_msg}
                    results['errors'].append(error_msg)
                    self.metrics['errors'].append(error_msg)
                    results['success'] = False
                    
                    # Continue with other sources
                    continue
            
            # Generate reports if configured
            if self.config.reporting:
                self._generate_reports()
            
            self.metrics['end_time'] = datetime.now()
            duration = (self.metrics['end_time'] - self.metrics['start_time']).total_seconds()
            
            self.logger.log_operation_end("pipeline_execution", success=results['success'], {
                'duration_seconds': duration,
                'sources_processed': self.metrics['sources_processed'],
                'total_records': self.metrics['records_processed'],
                'errors': len(self.metrics['errors'])
            })
            
            return {
                'success': results['success'],
                'metrics': self.metrics,
                'results': results
            }
            
        except Exception as e:
            self.metrics['end_time'] = datetime.now()
            error_msg = f"Pipeline execution failed: {str(e)}"
            self.logger.logger.error(error_msg)
            self.logger.logger.error(traceback.format_exc())
            
            return {
                'success': False,
                'error': error_msg,
                'metrics': self.metrics
            }
    
    def _process_source(self, source_config: Dict) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Process a single data source through all stages."""
        source_name = source_config['name']
        source_type = source_config['type']
        
        result = {
            'records_processed': 0,
            'records_valid': 0,
            'records_rejected': 0,
            'validation_failures': 0,
            'transformation_applied': False,
            'warehouse_table': None
        }
        
        # Stage 1: Ingestion
        self.logger.log_operation_start(f"ingestion", {'source': source_name})
        ingestion_source = get_ingestion_source(source_type, source_name, source_config)
        
        with ingestion_source:
            df = ingestion_source.extract()
            result['records_processed'] = len(df)
            self.metrics['records_processed'] += len(df)
        
        self.logger.log_operation_end(f"ingestion", success=True, {
            'records': len(df),
            'columns': list(df.columns)
        })
        
        # Stage 2: Validation
        self.logger.log_operation_start(f"validation", {'source': source_name})
        validation_config = source_config.get('validation_rules', [])
        
        # Convert validation rules to config format
        val_config = {
            'required_fields': source_config.get('schema', {}).get('required', list(df.columns)),
            'null_threshold': self.config.quality['thresholds'].get('null_percentage', 0.1),
            'duplicate_threshold': self.config.quality['thresholds'].get('duplicate_rate', 0.05)
        }
        
        validation_results = self.validator.run_all_checks(df, val_config)
        validation_summary = self.validator.get_summary()
        
        # Check for critical failures
        critical_failures = [r for r in validation_results if not r.passed and r.severity == "ERROR"]
        if critical_failures:
            self.logger.logger.error(f"Critical validation failures for {source_name}")
            for failure in critical_failures:
                self.logger.logger.error(f"  - {failure.check_name}: {failure.details}")
            result['validation_failures'] = len(critical_failures)
        
        result['records_valid'] = len(df) - result['records_rejected']
        self.logger.log_operation_end(f"validation", success=len(critical_failures) == 0, {
            'total_checks': validation_summary['total_checks'],
            'passed': validation_summary['passed'],
            'failed': validation_summary['failed']
        })
        
        # Stage 3: Transformation
        self.logger.log_operation_start(f"transformation", {'source': source_name})
        
        # Apply standard transformations
        df = DataTransformer.clean_column_names(df)
        df = DataTransformer.add_audit_columns(df)
        
        result['transformation_applied'] = True
        self.logger.log_operation_end(f"transformation", success=True, {
            'final_columns': list(df.columns)
        })
        
        # Stage 4: Load to Warehouse
        self.logger.log_operation_start(f"warehouse_load", {'source': source_name})
        
        # Find destination table
        dest_table = None
        for table_config in self.config.destination.get('tables', []):
            if source_name.replace('_data', '') in table_config['name']:
                dest_table = table_config
                break
        
        if dest_table:
            schema_name = dest_table.get('schema', 'analytics')
            table_name = dest_table['name']
            
            self.warehouse.create_schema(schema_name)
            self.warehouse.create_table(schema_name, table_name, df, if_exists="replace")
            
            result['warehouse_table'] = f"{schema_name}.{table_name}"
            self.logger.log_operation_end(f"warehouse_load", success=True, {
                'table': result['warehouse_table'],
                'records': len(df)
            })
        else:
            self.logger.logger.warning(f"No destination table configured for {source_name}")
        
        return result
    
    def _generate_reports(self):
        """Generate configured reports."""
        self.logger.log_operation_start("report_generation")
        
        output_dir = Path(self.config.reporting['output_dir'])
        output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        
        for dashboard in self.config.reporting.get('dashboards', []):
            try:
                report_name = dashboard['name']
                query_path = dashboard['query']
                
                # For now, generate a simple summary report
                timestamp = datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d_%H%M%S")
                report_file = output_dir / f"{report_name}_{timestamp}.csv"
                
                # Get warehouse summary
                summary = self.warehouse.create_analytics_summary()
                
                # Save summary as JSON
                import json
                json_file = output_dir / f"pipeline_summary_{timestamp}.json"
                with open(json_file, 'w') as f:
                    json.dump(summary, f, indent=2, default=str)
                
                self.logger.logger.info(f"Generated report: {report_file}")
                
            except Exception as e:
                self.logger.logger.error(f"Error generating report {dashboard['name']}: {e}")
        
        self.logger.log_operation_end("report_generation", success=True)
    
    def get_status(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Get current pipeline status and metrics."""
        return {
            'initialized': self.config is not None,
            'config': {
                'name': self.config.name if self.config else None,
                'version': self.config.version if self.config else None,
                'environment': self.config.environment if self.config else None

@app.get("/tables/{schema}/{table_name}")
async def get_table_data(
    schema: str,
    table_name: str,
    limit: int = Query(100, ge=1, le=10000),
    offset: int = Query(0, ge=0),
    wh: DataWarehouse = Depends(get_warehouse)
):
    """Get data from a specific table."""
    try:
        full_name = f"{schema}.{table_name}"
        
        # Get total count
        count_result = wh.fetch_dataframe(f"SELECT COUNT(*) as total FROM {full_name}")
        total = count_result['total'].iloc[0]
        
        # Get data
        query = f"SELECT * FROM {full_name} LIMIT {limit} OFFSET {offset}"
        df = wh.fetch_dataframe(query)
        
        return {
            "table": full_name,
            "total_rows": int(total),
            "limit": limit,
            "offset": offset,
            "columns": list(df.columns),
            "data": df.to_dict('records')
        }
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Error fetching table {schema}.{table_name}: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=500, detail=str(e))


@app.post("/query", response_model=QueryResult)
async def execute_query(
    query_request: Dict[str, Any],
    wh: DataWarehouse = Depends(get_warehouse)
):
    """Execute a custom SQL query (read-only)."""
    import time
    
    query = query_request.get('query', '')
    
    # Safety check - only allow SELECT queries
    query_upper = query.strip().upper()
    if not query_upper.startswith('SELECT'):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Only SELECT queries are allowed")
    
    try:
        start_time = time.time()
        df = wh.fetch_dataframe(query)
        execution_time = (time.time() - start_time) * 1000
        
        # Limit results to prevent memory issues
        if len(df) > 10000:
            df = df.head(10000)
        
        return QueryResult(
            query=query,
            row_count=len(df),
            columns=list(df.columns),
            data=df.to_dict('records'),
            execution_time_ms=execution_time
        )
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Query execution error: {e}")
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail=str(e))
